body:
Fairs as living cultural heritage

Traditional fairs, commonly called melas, are an important part of Gujarat's living cultural heritage. They bring communities together for religious worship, seasonal celebrations, social interaction, trade and entertainment.

Many fairs are associated with temples, sacred rivers or particular festivals. Others preserve tribal customs, traditional marriage practices or regional craftsmanship. A single fair may serve several of these purposes.

Understanding the traditional calendar

Most traditional fairs follow the Hindu lunar calendar rather than fixed Gregorian calendar dates. Consequently, their English calendar dates may change from year to year.

A tithi is a lunar calendar day. Each lunar month has a waxing fortnight and a waning fortnight.

Gujarati calendar termEquivalent termMeaning
SudShukla PakshaWaxing fortnight
VadKrishna PakshaWaning fortnight
PoonamPurnimaFull moon
AmasAmavasyaNew moon

Several Gujarati month names have corresponding Sanskrit names. Recognising these equivalents helps in answering questions that use different calendar terminology.

Gujarati monthAlternative nameApproximate Gregorian period
BhadarvoBhadrapadaAugust-September
KartakKartikaOctober-November
MahaMaghaJanuary-February
FaganPhalgunaFebruary-March
ChaitraChaitraMarch-April

These Gregorian periods are approximate. Lunar calendar adjustments may cause particular fairs to fall outside their most common English calendar month.

Tarnetar Fair

The Tarnetar Fair is held at Tarnetar village near Thangadh in Surendranagar district. Its religious centre is the Trinetreshwar Mahadev Temple, also known as Triniteshwar Mahadev Temple, dedicated to Shiva.

The traditional fair takes place on Bhadarva Sud 4, 5 and 6, generally during August or September.

Religious and legendary associations

According to local tradition, Tarnetar is associated with the swayamvara of Draupadi described in the Mahabharata. A swayamvara was a traditional arrangement through which a woman selected her husband from eligible suitors. The association with Draupadi is a local legend rather than an established historical identification of the event's location.

Communities and distinctive features

The fair has traditionally attracted Kolis, Rabaris, Bharwads, Kathis and other communities of Saurashtra. It is particularly associated with social gatherings and the traditional selection of marriage partners.

Decorated umbrellas carried by young men are among its most recognisable features. These umbrellas display colourful embroidery and mirror work. Folk dances, traditional costumes, ornaments and handicraft stalls are also important attractions.

Associate Tarnetar with Surendranagar, Bhadrapada, Trinetreshwar Mahadev, embroidered umbrellas and traditional matchmaking.

Prelims focus

  • Tarnetar is near Thangadh in Surendranagar district.
  • Its traditional dates are Bhadarva Sud 4 to 6.
  • The fair centres on Trinetreshwar Mahadev Temple.
  • It is associated with decorated umbrellas and traditional matchmaking.
  • Trap: Tarnetar is not a Kartik Purnima fair.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Social Science, Standard 10, English medium, 2020 reprint, Chapter 1, Heritage of India, printed pp. 3-4; Government of Gujarat, NRI Division, Trinetreshwar Mahadev Fair, When and Where; Gujarat Tourism, Tarnetar Fair, At a Glance and Who Comes. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026. The project-volume chapters could not be fully retrieved in readable form; the publicly available textbook edition and official sources provide the factual foundation.]

title: Gujarat's Traditional Fairs and the Tarnetar Fair

body:
Vautha Fair

The Vautha Fair is held at Vautha village in Dholka taluka of Ahmedabad district. It is especially famous for animal trading and pilgrimage at a sacred river confluence.

Time and sacred geography

The principal occasion is Kartik Purnima, the full moon of the Gujarati month of Kartak, generally falling in November. The fair commonly extends over several days around this occasion.

Vautha is situated at the confluence of the Sabarmati and Vatrak rivers. The wider river system is traditionally regarded as a Saptasangam, or meeting of 7 sacred rivers.

The 7 rivers associated with this sacred confluence are the Sabarmati, Vatrak, Meshwo, Hathmati, Shedhi, Majum and Khari. The Vatrak receives other rivers before meeting the Sabarmati.

According to religious tradition, Kartikeya, the son of Shiva, visited this sacred site. Pilgrims bathe in the river waters on Kartik Purnima.

Animal trading and participating communities

Vautha is particularly associated with the trading of donkeys and camels. Donkeys are often decorated before being brought to the fair. Farmers, animal traders, pastoral communities and pilgrims participate in the gathering.

Traditional participants include Jath and Vanjara communities and other pastoral groups. The fair also attracts villagers from the surrounding agricultural regions.

Vautha combines a sacred river pilgrimage with an important livestock market. Donkey trading is its distinctive economic feature.

Shamlaji Fair

The Shamlaji Fair, also known as the Shamlaji-Thakorji Fair, takes place at the Vishnu temple of Shamlaji in Shamlaji taluka of Aravalli district. The temple stands on the banks of the Meshwo River near the Gujarat-Rajasthan border.

Time and religious significance

The fair is centred on Kartik Purnima. Its traditional dates include Kartik Sud 11 to Poonam, although the wider period of pilgrimage and celebrations may be longer.

Shamlaji is a form of Vishnu, also associated with the names Gadadhar and Sakshi Gopal. Among local tribal devotees, the deity is affectionately known as Kaliyo Dev or Kaliyo Thakor.

Community association

The Bhil community has a particularly strong religious association with Shamlaji. The fair also attracts other devotees from Gujarat and neighbouring Rajasthan.

Pilgrimage, devotional singing, bathing in the Meshwo River and the purchase of ornaments and household articles are important aspects of the gathering.

Shamlaji's district

Shamlaji is in Aravalli district, not present-day Sabarkantha district. Aravalli was formed from Sabarkantha on 15 August 2013. Older geographical descriptions may therefore associate Shamlaji with Sabarkantha.

Distinguishing the 2 Kartik Purnima fairs

AttributeVauthaShamlaji
DistrictAhmedabadAravalli
Water bodySabarmati-Vatrak confluenceMeshwo River
Religious associationKartikeya and sacred bathingVishnu
Distinctive featureDonkey and camel tradingTemple pilgrimage
CommunitiesPastoral groups and tradersBhils and other devotees

Prelims focus

  • Both Vautha and Shamlaji are associated with Kartik Purnima.
  • Vautha is in Dholka taluka of Ahmedabad district.
  • Vautha is famous for Saptasangam and donkey trading.
  • Shamlaji is a Vishnu pilgrimage centre on the Meshwo River.
  • Shamlaji has a strong association with Bhil devotees.
  • Trap: Shamlaji belongs to Aravalli district, not present-day Sabarkantha.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Social Science, Standard 10, English medium, 2020 reprint, Chapter 1, printed p. 4; Government of Gujarat, NRI Division, Vautha Mela and Shamlaji Mela; Ministry of Tourism, Utsav, Shamlaji Fair; Aravalli District Administration, Shamlaji Temple and History. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Vautha and its Saptasangam tradition.

title: Vautha and Shamlaji: The Kartik Purnima Fairs

body:
Bhavnath Fair

The Bhavnath Fair, also known as the Mahashivratri Mela, is held at the Bhavnath Mahadev Temple at Girnar Taleti in Junagadh district. Girnar Taleti refers to the foothills of Mount Girnar.

The temple is dedicated to Shiva. The fair is one of the important religious gatherings associated with the sacred landscape of Girnar.

Time of celebration

The fair is associated with the waning fortnight of Maha, or Magha, and culminates in Mahashivratri, generally during February or March.

Mahashivratri is observed on the 14th lunar day of the waning fortnight, known as Maha Vad 14 in the Gujarati calendar.

The celebrations extend over several days. The traditional fair-date range is not described uniformly in published accounts: the 2020 state-board textbook lists Magh Vad 9 to 12, whereas the Gujarat Government's NRI Division describes a 5-day gathering beginning on Magh Vad 11. The decisive religious association is Mahashivratri.

Religious practices and communities

A distinctive feature of the Bhavnath Fair is the gathering of Naga sadhus, ascetics belonging to Hindu religious traditions. Their procession and ritual bathing at Mrigi Kund are important features of the Mahashivratri celebration.

The fair attracts pilgrims from different regions. Among the local communities, the Ahirs and Mers of the Junagadh region are traditionally prominent participants.

Bhavnath is primarily a Shaivite pilgrimage fair associated with Girnar, Mahashivratri and Naga sadhus.

Dang Darbar

The Dang Darbar is held at Ahwa, the district headquarters of Dang district, in the tribal region of southern Gujarat.

Time of celebration

It is associated with the Gujarati month of Fagan and the festival of Holi. The traditional gathering is generally organised during the days leading up to Holi, around Fagan Sud Poonam, usually in March.

Historical significance

The word darbar refers to a formal court or assembly. The Dang Darbar preserves the tradition of assemblies involving the tribal rulers and village chiefs of the Dangs during the British period.

The gathering continues as an occasion to recognise the historical position of local tribal rulers and chiefs, while celebrating the cultural identity of the region.

Participating communities

The celebrations feature the traditional clothing, folk music and dances of the tribal communities of the Dangs. Important participating communities include Bhils, Kunbis, Warlis and Gamits.

Unlike a fair centred on a particular temple deity, the Dang Darbar is distinguished by its historical association with tribal leadership and community gatherings.

Essential distinction

Bhavnath and Dang Darbar generally fall within the late-winter and early-spring festival season. Their religious and cultural foundations, however, are different. Bhavnath is associated with Shiva worship and Mahashivratri, whereas Dang Darbar is associated with tribal rulers, chiefs and the period immediately preceding Holi.

Prelims focus

  • Bhavnath Fair is held at the foothills of Girnar in Junagadh.
  • Its principal occasion is Mahashivratri in Maha Vad.
  • Naga sadhus and Mrigi Kund are associated with Bhavnath.
  • Dang Darbar takes place at Ahwa in Dang district.
  • Dang Darbar preserves the tradition of tribal assemblies and is held around Holi, generally before it.
  • Trap: Dang Darbar is not the Rathwa fair of Kavant.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Social Science, Standard 10, English medium, 2020 reprint, Chapter 1, printed p. 4; Government of Gujarat, NRI Division, Bhavnath Mahadev Mela, When and Who Comes; Gujarat Tourism, Mahashivratri Mela and Dang Darbar, At a Glance, When, Where and Who Comes. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Mahashivratri and the pre-Holi tribal gathering.

title: Bhavnath Fair and Dang Darbar: Celebrations Before Holi

body:
Holi and the tribal fair season

Holi is an important occasion for several tribal communities of eastern and northern Gujarat. The period following Holi includes traditional fairs that bring people together for social interaction, trade, celebrations and customary rituals.

Kavant, Gol Gadheda and Chitra-Vichitra are distinct gatherings. Although all 3 are associated with the Holi season, their places, timing and principal customs differ.

Kavant Fair

The Kavant Fair is held at Kavant, also written as Kawant or Kwant, in Chhota Udepur district. It is especially associated with the Rathwa tribal community, also written as Rathva.

Time and significance

The fair generally begins on the 3rd day after Holi, during the Fagan festival season. It is closely connected with the harvest, nature and community celebrations.

Rathwa communities gather to celebrate through folk music and dance, meet relatives, discuss marriage arrangements and exchange goods. Participants also arrive from neighbouring states.

The state-board fair table associates Kwant with the Bhanguriya fair during the period from Holi to Rang Panchami. Rang Panchami refers to the 5th lunar day of the waning fortnight after the Holi full moon. The central identification remains Kavant, Chhota Udepur and Rathwa culture.

Kavant is particularly associated with the Rathwa community, rather than the Bhil-Garasia association of Chitra-Vichitra.

Gol Gadheda Fair

The Gol Gadheda Fair, also called Godh Gadheda no Melo, is held at Jesawada village in Garbada taluka of Dahod district.

Time and community

The fair takes place after Holi, during the Fagan festival season, usually in March. Traditional descriptions commonly place it about 5 to 7 days after Holi, although local observances may also occur later.

It is a tribal fair of the Dahod region, where Bhil cultural traditions are particularly prominent.

Distinctive custom

A traditional competition involves young men attempting to obtain jaggery placed at the top of a wooden pole while young women create obstacles around it. The custom was historically associated with the selection of marriage partners.

The word gol refers to jaggery, while gadheda refers to a donkey. The name reflects the traditional competition rather than the commercial sale of donkeys. Its historical marriage association should not be understood as a compulsory marriage arrangement in contemporary celebrations.

Gol Gadheda is a tribal customary fair in Dahod. Vautha is the well-known livestock trading fair involving donkeys in Ahmedabad district.

Chitra-Vichitra Fair

The Chitra-Vichitra Fair is held at Gunbhakhari village near Khedbrahma in Sabarkantha district, close to the Rajasthan border. The village is also written as Gunbhankhari and lies in Poshina taluka.

The fair takes place at a sacred Triveni Sangam, traditionally identified as the meeting of the Sabarmati, Akul and Vyakul rivers.

Time of celebration

The gathering occurs approximately 2 weeks after Holi, around the new moon at the end of Fagan Vad. It generally falls in March or April.

The celebrations begin around the eve of Amavasya, distinguishing Chitra-Vichitra from fairs held on Purnima.

Communities and customary practices

The fair is especially associated with the Bhils and Garasias of northern Gujarat and neighbouring Rajasthan.

Its distinctive feature is the combination of remembrance and celebration. During the night preceding the main fair, women gather near the river to mourn deceased relatives. The following day is marked by folk music, dancing, trade and social interaction.

The gathering also provides opportunities for young people to meet prospective marriage partners. Its name is traditionally associated with the Mahabharata figures Chitrangada and Vichitravirya, referred to in local fair traditions as Chitra and Vichitra.

Sequence of the post-Holi fairs

FairDistrictPrincipal communityDistinctive association
KavantChhota UdepurRathwaHarvest and community celebration
Gol GadhedaDahodLocal tribal communities, especially the Bhil regionJaggery-pole competition
Chitra-VichitraSabarkanthaBhil and GarasiaRemembrance of deceased relatives and matchmaking

Prelims focus

  • Kavant is associated with the Rathwas of Chhota Udepur.
  • Gol Gadheda takes place at Jesawada in Garbada taluka of Dahod.
  • Chitra-Vichitra takes place at Gunbhakhari near Khedbrahma in Sabarkantha.
  • Chitra-Vichitra is associated with Bhils, Garasias and the remembrance of deceased relatives.
  • Chitra-Vichitra occurs near Amavasya approximately 2 weeks after Holi.
  • Trap: Gol Gadheda is not the donkey trading fair of Vautha.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Social Science, Standard 10, English medium, 2020 reprint, Chapter 1, printed p. 4; Gujarat Tourism, Kavant Fair and Chitra Vichitra Fair; Ministry of Tourism, Incredible India, Gol Gadheda Fair; Dahod District Administration, Culture and Heritage; Ministry of Tourism, Utsav, Chitra Vichitra Fair, organiser and venue details; DeshGujarat, Chitra Vichitra Fair 2013 on 10-11 April in Tribal North Gujarat, 9 April 2013. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]
